lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Chapter Five · New Hampshire|William Plumer · Dartmouth's state

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Concord, New Hampshire. June 1816. A new governor takes office, and within weeks the state does something that sounds radical even now. It rewrites the charter of its elite private college and puts it under public control.
lines.caption: Concord, New Hampshire. June 1816. A new governor takes office, and within weeks the state does something that sounds radical even now. It rewrites the charter of its elite private college and puts it under public control.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Dartmouth College becomes, by law, Dartmouth University. State-appointed trustees. A state board of overseers. The new university moves into the college buildings in Hanover.
lines.caption: Dartmouth College becomes, by law, Dartmouth University. State-appointed trustees. A state board of overseers. The new university moves into the college buildings in Hanover.

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: Big Green, greetings from Hanover! And yes, for a while there were two Dartmouths in one little town.
lines.caption: Big Green, greetings from Hanover! And yes, for a while there were two Dartmouths in one little town.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Two governors in Rhode Island, two Dartmouths in New Hampshire. You people really like doubles.
lines.caption: Two governors in Rhode Island, two Dartmouths in New Hampshire. You people really like doubles.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The governor in that chair was New Hampshire's number seven. William Plumer.
lines.caption: The governor in that chair was New Hampshire's number seven. William Plumer.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: William Plumer was born June 25th, 1759, in Newburyport, Massachusetts. His family moved to Epping, New Hampshire, in 1768, when he was eight or nine. He did not go to college.
lines.caption: William Plumer was born June 25th, 1759, in Newburyport, Massachusetts. His family moved to Epping, New Hampshire, in 1768, when he was eight or nine. He did not go to college.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Before he was a lawyer, he was a Baptist lay preacher. Then he studied law and went into politics. He never sat in a college classroom. Later, he went after one.
lines.caption: Before he was a lawyer, he was a Baptist lay preacher. Then he studied law and went into politics. He never sat in a college classroom. Later, he went after one.
lines.visual: card:Fact 1 of 7|A Baptist lay preacher before he became a lawyer · no college

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: A preacher, a lawyer, then a governor. Very North Country. You do whatever the season needs.
lines.caption: A preacher, a lawyer, then a governor. Very North Country. You do whatever the season needs.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He was Speaker of the New Hampshire House in 1791 and 1797. In 1802 he went to the United States Senate as a Federalist.
lines.caption: He was Speaker of the New Hampshire House in 1791 and 1797. In 1802 he went to the United States Senate as a Federalist.
lines.visual: card:Fact 2 of 7|Speaker of the New Hampshire House, 1791 and 1797

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1803, when Jefferson bought Louisiana, some New England Federalists talked about leaving the Union. Plumer was one of them. Years later he called it the greatest political error of his life.
lines.caption: In 1803, when Jefferson bought Louisiana, some New England Federalists talked about leaving the Union. Plumer was one of them. Years later he called it the greatest political error of his life.
lines.visual: card:Fact 3 of 7|He joined the 1803 secession talk, and later called it his greatest error

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Okay, a guy who admits he was wrong. I like him already.
lines.caption: Okay, a guy who admits he was wrong. I like him already.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now, the count. From 1784 to 1792 New Hampshire's chief executive was called President, not Governor. The standard list counts those presidents anyway. Meshech Weare, John Langdon, John Sullivan, Josiah Bartlett. Then John Taylor Gilman, Jeremiah Smith. And seven, Plumer.
lines.caption: Now, the count. From 1784 to 1792 New Hampshire's chief executive was called President, not Governor. The standard list counts those presidents anyway. Meshech Weare, John Langdon, John Sullivan, Josiah Bartlett. Then John Taylor Gilman, Jeremiah Smith. And seven, Plumer.
lines.visual: card:Fact 4 of 7|Counting the early presidents, Plumer is New Hampshire's 7th governor

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: New Hampshire gives each person just one number, so Plumer's two runs, 1812 to 1813 and 1816 to 1819, both count as seven. Count only from the 1792 title of governor, and seven becomes Levi Woodbury.
lines.caption: New Hampshire gives each person just one number, so Plumer's two runs, 1812 to 1813 and 1816 to 1819, both count as seven. Count only from the 1792 title of governor, and seven becomes Levi Woodbury.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: And John Sullivan up there is the brother of the Massachusetts guy?
lines.caption: And John Sullivan up there is the brother of the Massachusetts guy?

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Same family, Gary. James was Massachusetts number seven. His brother John was New Hampshire number three.
lines.caption: Same family, Gary. James was Massachusetts number seven. His brother John was New Hampshire number three.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: So, Dartmouth. When Plumer came back in 1816, the college was in a feud between its president, John Wheelock, and its trustees. The state stepped in. The 1816 law reinstated Wheelock, added trustees, and gave the governor power over appointments.
lines.caption: So, Dartmouth. When Plumer came back in 1816, the college was in a feud between its president, John Wheelock, and its trustees. The state stepped in. The 1816 law reinstated Wheelock, added trustees, and gave the governor power over appointments.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The college's old trustees sued the state-approved secretary of the new board, William H. Woodward. The case went to the United States Supreme Court. Daniel Webster, Dartmouth class of 1801, argued for the college.
lines.caption: The college's old trustees sued the state-approved secretary of the new board, William H. Woodward. The case went to the United States Supreme Court. Daniel Webster, Dartmouth class of 1801, argued for the college.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1819, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled for the college. A charter, he said, is a contract, and the Constitution forbids a state from breaking a contract. Dartmouth University disappeared.
lines.caption: In 1819, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled for the college. A charter, he said, is a contract, and the Constitution forbids a state from breaking a contract. Dartmouth University disappeared.
lines.visual: card:Fact 5 of 7|Dartmouth College v. Woodward, 1819 · the state lost

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: Stay green. Though honestly, the state wanted the college to answer to the public. That's not a crazy idea.
lines.caption: Stay green. Though honestly, the state wanted the college to answer to the public. That's not a crazy idea.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And here's the twist. That ruling reached far beyond Hanover. It told private corporations that their charters were contracts the states could not easily touch. States later learned to write in the right to change charters, but the case set the terms for generations.
lines.caption: And here's the twist. That ruling reached far beyond Hanover. It told private corporations that their charters were contracts the states could not easily touch. States later learned to write in the right to change charters, but the case set the terms for generations.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The case is called Trustees of Dartmouth College versus Woodward. And Webster's argument is remembered for one line, recorded later: It is, sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it.
lines.caption: The case is called Trustees of Dartmouth College versus Woodward. And Webster's argument is remembered for one line, recorded later: It is, sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it.
lines.visual: card:Daniel Webster, 1818|"It is, sir, a small college" · as recalled by a listener years later

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: We put that line on everything, Gary. Mugs. Sweaters. Probably a canoe.
lines.caption: We put that line on everything, Gary. Mugs. Sweaters. Probably a canoe.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: So the little college beat the whole state.
lines.caption: So the little college beat the whole state.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The little college beat the whole state, and corporations everywhere got a shield. That's not a small thing, Gary. That's the kind of ruling bank lawyers and railroad lawyers would cite for the next century.
lines.caption: The little college beat the whole state, and corporations everywhere got a shield. That's not a small thing, Gary. That's the kind of ruling bank lawyers and railroad lawyers would cite for the next century.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And look at what the college was chartered to do. Dartmouth's 1769 charter names the education of youth of the Indian tribes as a purpose. A Mohegan minister, Samson Occom, raised more than twelve thousand pounds in Britain to fund that mission.
lines.caption: And look at what the college was chartered to do. Dartmouth's 1769 charter names the education of youth of the Indian tribes as a purpose. A Mohegan minister, Samson Occom, raised more than twelve thousand pounds in Britain to fund that mission.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Occom crossed to Britain with Nathaniel Whitaker in 1766. He preached across Britain from February 1766 to July 1767, raising money from congregations that came to see a Native minister in person. Wheelock had promised the money for a school for Native students.
lines.caption: Occom crossed to Britain with Nathaniel Whitaker in 1766. He preached across Britain from February 1766 to July 1767, raising money from congregations that came to see a Native minister in person. Wheelock had promised the money for a school for Native students.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Dartmouth's royal charter came on December 13th, 1769, from New Hampshire's colonial governor, John Wentworth, in the name of King George the Third. The charter's purposes put the Indian tribes first. The student body didn't.
lines.caption: Dartmouth's royal charter came on December 13th, 1769, from New Hampshire's colonial governor, John Wentworth, in the name of King George the Third. The charter's purposes put the Indian tribes first. The student body didn't.

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: Hanover in the snow is beautiful. But the man who raised the money deserved a better school than the one he got.
lines.caption: Hanover in the snow is beautiful. But the man who raised the money deserved a better school than the one he got.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Eleazar Wheelock used that money to found Dartmouth. And in its first two hundred years, nineteen Native American students graduated. It wasn't until 1970, under President John Kemeny, that Dartmouth officially recommitted to its founding mission.
lines.caption: Eleazar Wheelock used that money to found Dartmouth. And in its first two hundred years, nineteen Native American students graduated. It wasn't until 1970, under President John Kemeny, that Dartmouth officially recommitted to its founding mission.
lines.visual: card:Fact 6 of 7|In Dartmouth's first 200 years, 19 Native American students graduated

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Twelve thousand pounds raised by a Native preacher, and nineteen graduates in two hundred years.
lines.caption: Twelve thousand pounds raised by a Native preacher, and nineteen graduates in two hundred years.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He lost. The trustees won. And the people the college was chartered to serve were mostly left outside.
lines.caption: He lost. The trustees won. And the people the college was chartered to serve were mostly left outside.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1820, Plumer was a presidential elector. Every other elector in the country voted for James Monroe. Plumer alone voted for John Quincy Adams.
lines.caption: In 1820, Plumer was a presidential elector. Every other elector in the country voted for James Monroe. Plumer alone voted for John Quincy Adams.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In that same 1820 vote, Plumer also declined to vote for the vice president, Daniel Tompkins. One elector, alone against the whole country, twice in one ballot.
lines.caption: In that same 1820 vote, Plumer also declined to vote for the vice president, Daniel Tompkins. One elector, alone against the whole country, twice in one ballot.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: His son, William Plumer Junior, went to Congress from 1819 to 1825. Plumer was elected to the American Antiquarian Society in 1815. He spent his old age writing, collecting, and keeping records of the men he'd served with.
lines.caption: His son, William Plumer Junior, went to Congress from 1819 to 1825. Plumer was elected to the American Antiquarian Society in 1815. He spent his old age writing, collecting, and keeping records of the men he'd served with.
lines.visual: card:William Plumer, historian|First president of the New Hampshire Historical Society

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: Okay. Preacher, senator, secession guy, sorry about the secession, takes on a college, loses, votes alone, writes history till ninety-one. That's a full life.
lines.caption: Okay. Preacher, senator, secession guy, sorry about the secession, takes on a college, loses, votes alone, writes history till ninety-one. That's a full life.

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: That's New Hampshire, Gary. Live free and argue with everybody.
lines.caption: That's New Hampshire, Gary. Live free and argue with everybody.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He became the first president of the New Hampshire Historical Society. He died on December 22nd, 1850, at ninety-one. At the time he was the oldest living former governor in the country, and the oldest governor America had ever had.
lines.caption: He became the first president of the New Hampshire Historical Society. He died on December 22nd, 1850, at ninety-one. At the time he was the oldest living former governor in the country, and the oldest governor America had ever had.
lines.visual: card:Fact 7 of 7|The lone 1820 elector against Monroe · died at 91, the oldest governor ever

lines.speaker: DA
lines.say: The lone dissenter. A very New Hampshire thing to be. Hollis out.
lines.caption: The lone dissenter. A very New Hampshire thing to be. Hollis out.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He lost. The trustees won. Ask who that ruling is still protecting.
lines.caption: He lost. The trustees won. Ask who that ruling is still protecting.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: New Hampshire. Keep it real.
lines.caption: New Hampshire. Keep it real.
